title: The Invention of the Light Bulb
summary: How Thomas Edison and earlier inventors solved the problem of dangerous, short-lived candlelight by inventing a safe, long-lasting electric light bulb.
poll: The invention of the light bulb changed daily life more than almost any other invention in history.

versions.title: The Invention of the Light Bulb
versions.text:
Long ago, homes had no light bulbs. People used candles. Candles were not safe. They could start fires.

A man named Edison worked hard. He made a bulb. It could glow. His bulb used a thin wire. The wire got hot. It made light.

Edison was not alone. Other men tried too. One man was named Swan. He lived in England. He made a bulb too.

Edison tried many things. He tried cotton. He tried wood. At last, he found a good wire. It did not burn fast.

Edison's bulb could glow a long time. This was new. Soon, homes got light bulbs. People did not need candles.

Today, we use light bulbs. We flip a switch. Light comes on fast. We thank Edison for his hard work.

versions.title: The Invention of the Light Bulb
versions.text:
Long before light bulbs, people lit candles and oil lamps at night. These open flames were not safe. A single spark could start a fire and burn down a house. Many families lost everything this way.

Thomas Edison wanted to build a better, longer-lasting light. He worked in a busy lab with a team of helpers. Edison tested hundreds of materials and wrote down every result. He never gave up, even after many failures.

Edison was not the only inventor working on this idea. Years before him, other men had built early light bulbs too. A British inventor named Joseph Swan made a working bulb at about the same time. Many people were racing toward the same goal.

After many tries, Edison found that a thin wire made of carbon worked best. We call this wire a filament. When power ran through it, the wire glowed for many hours. It did not burn out quickly like other wires.

Edison's bulb became famous because it was cheap and lasted a long time. Factories soon began making bulbs so that ordinary families could light their homes. Life after dark began to change.

Because of Edison and the inventors before him, people no longer needed open flames at night. Today, we flip a simple switch, and the room fills with light at once. His work still helps us every day.

Edison worked in his laboratory with a team of helpers, testing hundreds of materials until he found that a carbon filament could glow for many hours without burning out. Because the bulb was both affordable and long-lasting, factories began producing it for families everywhere, which changed how people lived and worked after dark.

questions.stem: Which statement best captures the central idea of this article?
options: Candles stayed the safest way to light a home
Joseph Swan's laboratory stood in the same city as Edison's
Edison and other inventors solved the problem of short-lived light through steady experimentation
Factories only grew important after electricity was invented
questions.why: The article centers on how persistent experimentation by Edison and fellow inventors solved the problem of dangerous, unreliable lighting.

wrong.A: The article presents candles as hazardous, not safe.
wrong.B: The article never states the two laboratories were in the same city.
wrong.D: Factories are discussed only in relation to producing light bulbs.

questions.stem: Based on the article, why were open flames considered hazardous?
options: They produced far too little light to be of any real use
They required an expensive fuel that few families could afford to buy
They could not safely be lit anywhere indoors at all
A single stray spark could ignite a destructive, fast-spreading fire

wrong.A: Candles and lamps did provide light; that was their purpose.
wrong.B: Fuel cost is not discussed in the article.
wrong.C: The article shows candles and lamps being used indoors.

questions.stem: What specific discovery allowed Edison's filament to perform so well?
options: It was coated in a special, protective layer of glass
It was made of a thin carbon wire that resisted burning out quickly
It used a careful mixture of candle wax and soft metal
It had been imported directly from Joseph Swan's own laboratory
questions.why: The article states that Edison discovered a thin carbon wire, the filament, that glowed for many hours without rapidly deteriorating.

wrong.A: A glass coating on the filament itself is not mentioned.
wrong.C: Candle wax is never described as part of the filament.
wrong.D: Swan built his own separate bulb; the article does not say Edison imported parts from him.

questions.stem: What can be inferred about the scientific process from how many materials Edison's team tested?
options: Edison managed to succeed on his very first careful attempt
Testing many materials is usually a waste of valuable time
Scientific progress often requires extensive trial and error before success
Only a single material has ever been tested for any invention
questions.why: Testing hundreds of materials before succeeding shows that scientific breakthroughs often come only after extensive trial and error.

wrong.A: The article describes countless failed attempts before success.
wrong.B: The article presents this testing as essential, not wasteful.
wrong.D: The article explicitly describes hundreds of different materials being tested.

questions.stem: Why does the article mention that inventors in multiple countries were racing toward the same prize?
options: To show that only a single country cared about electric light
To prove that Edison secretly stole ideas from other nations
To argue that this kind of competition always slows down progress
To suggest that competition and shared goals can drive innovation forward
questions.why: Mentioning inventors across countries racing toward the same goal suggests that shared ambition and competition pushed innovation forward.

wrong.A: The article shows inventors in several different countries caring about this problem.
wrong.B: The article never accuses Edison of stealing ideas.
wrong.C: The outcome in the article is rapid progress, not slower progress.

questions.stem: In the article, what does "durable" most precisely describe about the light bulb?
options: It could survive being dropped from very great heights
It could operate for a long time without breaking down
It could be repaired by almost anyone without any tools
It could slowly change colors depending on the weather
questions.why: The article uses "durable" to describe how the bulb could function for a long time without breaking down or wearing out.

wrong.A: Durability in the article refers to lasting use, not surviving drops.
wrong.C: Repair ease is never discussed in the article.
wrong.D: Color change is never mentioned in the article.

questions.stem: How does the article's structure support its central idea?
options: It presents the problem, the struggle to solve it, and the eventual impact in sequence
It randomly jumps between many unrelated topics with no clear order
It only ever describes Edison's own personal life story
It focuses entirely on comparing the prices of different bulbs
questions.why: The article's sequence, moving from the danger of candles, through experimentation, to lasting impact, reinforces its central idea about solving a real problem.

wrong.B: The structure follows a clear, logical order rather than jumping randomly.
wrong.C: Edison's personal life beyond his work is not the article's focus.
wrong.D: Price comparisons between bulbs are not discussed.

questions.stem: What effect did the combination of affordability and durability have on the light bulb's adoption?
options: It somehow made the bulb too expensive for factories to produce
It strangely limited the bulb to use only inside laboratories
It accidentally caused candles to become even more widely used
It allowed ordinary families everywhere to adopt it widely and fast
questions.why: Because the bulb was both affordable and durable, factories could mass-produce it, letting ordinary families adopt it widely and quickly.

wrong.A: Affordability made production and sale easier, not harder.
wrong.B: The article shows the bulb spreading into ordinary homes, not staying confined to laboratories.
wrong.C: The bulb replaced candles; it did not increase their use.

HIGH.prompt: Analyze how competition, failure, and persistence shaped the invention of the light bulb. Use evidence from the article to support your analysis.
checklist: Did you reference specific evidence, such as the filament or multiple inventors?
Did you explain the role of failure or repeated testing?
Did you connect the invention to its lasting impact on daily life?
HIGH.modelAnswer: The invention of the light bulb was shaped by competition, failure, and persistence working together. Several inventors, including Thomas Edison and Joseph Swan, were racing to solve the same problem: open flames from candles and oil lamps were hazardous and unreliable. Edison's laboratory tested hundreds of materials, failing repeatedly, before discovering that a carbon filament could glow reliably for many hours without deteriorating. This persistence, combined with competition from inventors across different countries, produced a bulb that was both affordable and durable enough for factories to manufacture on a large scale, ultimately transforming daily life by making safe, instant light something people now rarely even think about.

LOW.stem: What problem were Edison and other inventors all trying to solve?

MID.stem: Based on the article, what likely made Edison's filament better than earlier wires he tried?
options: It was the cheapest material he could find

MID.stem: Why might the article mention both Edison and Joseph Swan instead of only Edison?

HIGH.stem: What does the article imply about the relationship between scientific failure and eventual success?
